newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-BoE says City will reap rewards from EMU.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-BoE says City will reap rewards from EMU.

text.p: The City of London will reap rich rewards from a single European currency, whether Britain signs up or not, Bank of England Governor Eddie George said on Monday.
But he said while the political commitment in Germany and France to establish European economic and monetary union (EMU) in 1999 had increased, the economic conditions had become less favourable.

"Any major development carries risks and opportunities for the City but provided we are properly prepared, the opportunites outweigh the risks whether Britain is in or out," George told a news conference.

His upbeat comments were apparently intended to allay fears that the City could lose its role as Europe's leading financial centre if Britain exercised its "opt-out" from the single currency, the euro.
George noted that despite the uncertainty about Britain's involvement, many leading international banks were still moving into London.
"All of that seems to me to be strongly suggestive that we have a tremendous base to take advantage of the opportunities that the euro will present," he said.
Speaking at the launch of a Bank paper on "Practical Issues Arising from the Introduction of the Euro," George said he was confident that London would be ready by January 1, 1999.

However, the central bank chief expressed doubts about whether the new currency would be launched on schedule, describing the economic conditions as "somewhat unfavourable" despite the political commitment to EMU of German Chancellor Helmut Kohl and French President Jacques Chirac.
"Overall, I think there is a growing conviction that monetary union will occur, at least among a core group of countries from January 1, 1999," George said.
"I am concerned that the economic slowdown which has occurred across Europe...is actually making the economic condition more difficult for a decision to go ahead in the spring of 1998."
The Bank of England has adopted a scrupulously neutral stance on whether Britain should join EMU or not, saying that is a decision for politicians to make.
Government policy is to take part fully in preparations for EMU while deferring a decision on whether Britain should participate or not.
The right wing of the ruling Conservative party bitterly opposes the single currency as an unacceptable erosion of British sovereignty.
George also addressed outstanding technical issues which some bankers fear could impair the City's chances of retaining its disproportionately large share of international business.

French and German banks have said Britain should not get equal access to a new intra-day payments system known as Target or to euro-denominated liquidity during the trading day if it refuses to sign up to EMU.
George played down the importance of the issue, saying even if Britain were denied equal access to euro-liquidity there were other means to secure it.
"The Target issue is rather trivial. There are alternatives, but we will continue to pursue it as a point of principle," said George.
An opinion poll of 392 directors of companies listed on the London Stock Exchange showed 58.4 percent opposed monetary union on the grounds that it would be bad for the British economy.

"Even among the 37.2 percent who support the idea, there are plenty who think Britain should exercise its opt-out clause and postpone adoption of the euro beyond 1999," Hemmington Scott, who conducted the poll for accountants Price Waterhouse, said.
